levels.title: Your first local HTTP lab
levels.primer: A browser or curl sends an HTTP request to a server. The server returns a status code and a response body. You will observe both on your own computer.
levels.experiment: Serve one page on your own computer, request it with curl, then compare its successful response with a request for a page that does not exist.

levels.control: Stop your local server and repeat the same request. Explain why a connection failure differs from an HTTP 404 returned by a running server.
levels.recall: Without opening the walkthrough, explain 127.0.0.1, a port, a GET request, HTTP 200, HTTP 404 and a connection failure.

experiment_guidance.title: Serve a webpage and inspect two HTTP responses
experiment_guidance.brief: Build a tiny web server on your own computer and see what an HTTP request returns. Use two Ubuntu/Linux terminal windows, Python 3 and curl. No paid course, account, vulnerable app or cloud lab is needed.
experiment_guidance.done_when: You observed the page response and the missing-page response, explained the address and port in your own words, saved your observations in {lab_dir}/foundations-experiment.json, and stopped your practice server.
steps:
Prepare two terminal windows on the computer where you will run this lab. We will call them Terminal A and Terminal B. Your workspace is open. Run the commands below in your terminals; Ascend does not execute them automatically.

In Terminal A, check that both tools are available:
```sh
python3 --version
curl --version
```
A Python 3 version and a curl version mean you can continue. If a tool is missing, end this session and use the first hint to repair your setup before continuing practice.

In Terminal A, make a new temporary folder containing one page, then serve that folder on your own computer: ```sh lab_site=$(mktemp -d /tmp/ascend-http.XXXXXX) printf '

My first lab

\n' > "$lab_site/index.html" python3 -m http.server 8765 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory "$lab_site" ``` Leave this terminal running. A message beginning “Serving HTTP on 127.0.0.1” means the server started. 127.0.0.1 means this computer; 8765 is the port identifying this server. No public website is involved.

In Terminal B, request your page:
```sh
curl --noproxy "*" -i http://127.0.0.1:8765/
```
This sends a GET request for /. The -i option shows response headers as well as the body. Find the first HTTP line: expect status 200. Below the headers, find the page text “My first lab”. Also look at Terminal A: it should log this request. Record what you actually see.

In Terminal B, ask the same server for a page you did not create:
```sh
curl --noproxy "*" -i http://127.0.0.1:8765/missing-page
```
Expect status 404. The server is still running and answering; this path simply has no page. Compare the two status codes and response bodies. A 404 here is an expected observation, not a failed setup.

Save your observations from Terminal B. Copy this whole block. It asks for your actual results and your own short explanations, then creates the JSON report at the finish-line path. It does not supply the answers or overwrite an existing report.
```sh
python3 -c '
import json
from pathlib import Path
report = {
    "scope": "Only my own local practice server",
    "target": input("URL you requested: ").strip(),
    "home_status": input("Status code for /: ").strip(),
    "home_body": input("One line from the / response body: ").strip(),
    "missing_status": input("Status code for /missing-page: ").strip(),
    "loopback_meaning": input("What does 127.0.0.1 mean? ").strip(),
    "port_meaning": input("What is the port number for? ").strip(),
    "comparison": input("Why did the two requests give different responses? ").strip(),
    "limitations": input("What did this lab not test? ").strip()
}
if not all(report.values()):
    raise SystemExit("An answer was empty. No report saved; run again when ready.")
path = Path("{lab_dir}/foundations-experiment.json").expanduser()
path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
if path.exists():
    raise SystemExit("A report already exists. Open it in your text editor to update it.")
with path.open("x") as output:
    json.dump(report, output, indent=2)
print("Saved:", path)
'
```
If the report already exists, open it in your text editor to review or update your notes instead of replacing it. This exercise checks the file on the computer running Ascend. For a hosted/container server, the report must be placed at that server’s configured lab path; a file saved only on your laptop will not be visible to the checker.

Stop your practice server: return to Terminal A and press Ctrl+C. Keep your saved report.

Back in Ascend, open Challenge options → Check evidence to check that the report file is present. Then use Log progress, briefly describe what you learned, and select Mark as done when your report contains the observations and explanations above. This file check does not grade your reasoning and this task does not earn automatic XP.
hints: Ubuntu/Linux setup: if Python 3 or curl is missing, install the free packages with sudo apt update followed by sudo apt install python3 curl. If you need to repair setup, end the session before installing packages. No paid course is required.
“Address already in use” means port 8765 is occupied. Use 8766 in the server command and in BOTH curl URLs; do not stop an unrelated service.
“Connection refused” means curl could not reach a running server at that address/port. Check Terminal A and the URL. This differs from 404, which is a response from a running server.

A 200 response demonstrates that this page was served. It does not demonstrate a vulnerability, an exploit, authentication or authorization. This is the networking setup skill you will use in later security labs.

steps: Repeat the local page request on port 8766. Predict which part of the URL must change, then record the actual response. In Terminal A, reuse the folder and start: python3 -m http.server 8766 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory "$lab_site". If this is a new terminal, recreate the page folder using the previous challenge first.

In Terminal B, request the new address and record the actual response:
```sh
curl --noproxy "*" -i http://127.0.0.1:8766/
```
Explain which URL component changed and why.

Stop your local server and repeat the same request. Explain why a connection failure differs from an HTTP 404 returned by a running server.

Press Ctrl+C in Terminal A. Then run in Terminal B:
```sh
curl --noproxy "*" --max-time 3 -i http://127.0.0.1:8766/
```
A connection error after stopping the server is expected. There should be no HTTP status line from that stopped server.

Save your prediction, observations and explanation from Terminal B. Answer these prompts in your own words; use “none” if you used no help. Existing reports are kept.
```sh
python3 -c '
import json
from pathlib import Path
report = {
    "prediction": input("Before testing, what did you expect the port change to do? ").strip(),
    "changed_url": input("What URL did you request on port 8766? ").strip(),
    "running_response": input("What status and body did the running server return? ").strip(),
    "stopped_response": input("What did curl report after you stopped the server? ").strip(),
    "why_not_404": input("Why is that different from HTTP 404? ").strip(),
    "help_used": input("What notes or help did you use? ").strip(),
    "limitations": input("What did this test not establish? ").strip()
}
if not all(report.values()):
    raise SystemExit("An answer was empty. No report saved; run again when ready.")
path = Path("{lab_dir}/foundations-assessment.json").expanduser()
path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
if path.exists():
    raise SystemExit("A report already exists. Open it in your text editor to update it.")
with path.open("x") as output:
    json.dump(report, output, indent=2)
print("Saved:", path)
'
```
Leave the server stopped. Use Challenge options → Check evidence, then Log progress → Mark as done after reviewing your report. A reviewer or your honest self-review must assess the explanation; the file check alone cannot do that.

levels.title: Inspect and narrow permissions on a local file
levels.primer: Use the named inputs and environment in this level’s practice task. The scenario decision is a separate conceptual check.
levels.experiment: Use Linux, macOS or WSL for this filesystem exercise. Work only on the extracted permissions.txt file. Inspect your identity and its mode.
levels.variant: Change the training file to 640 and compare owner/group/other bits with 600. Record what a second-identity test would be needed to verify.
levels.control: Owner reading must still work; do not claim a runtime test as another user if you only inspected mode bits.
levels.recall: Explain the difference between authentication, authorization and process privilege.

case.prompt: A user can read a file but cannot traverse its parent directory.
case.correct: Parent-directory permissions can still prevent access by pathname.
case.incorrect: File read permission guarantees successful pathname access.

levels.title: Make a finding another person can verify
levels.primer: Use the named inputs and environment in this level’s practice task. The scenario decision is a separate conceptual check.

levels.title: Run a small authorized assessment
levels.primer: Use the named inputs and environment in this level’s practice task. The scenario decision is a separate conceptual check.
levels.experiment: Extract a fresh copy of service.py and scenario.json. Independently use note 2 (owner bob) and alice as the unrelated user. State the scope before starting.

case.prompt: No finding is reproduced during a bounded assessment.
case.correct: Report scope, tests and uncertainty; a justified negative result is legitimate.
case.incorrect: Report the target as secure without qualification.

levels.title: Recheck the boundary with a specified change
levels.primer: Use the named task files for the changed case. Predict the effect before opening previous notes.

levels.control: Bob must still read his own remaining test note; alice must not gain access to carol’s note.
levels.recall: Reconstruct why the specified input change did or did not change the outcome. State help used and what remains untested.

case.prompt: You reset your lab and solve the same exercise again using the same inputs and steps.
case.correct: You can repeat the solution. Try a changed input or environment to test whether you can adapt it.

tracks.entry: Understand service versions, asset ownership and the difference between an advisory and confirmed exposure.
tracks.limits: Use synthetic inventories and approved scan exports. EPSS estimates and KEV membership inform decisions but do not prove exploitation on your system.

levels.title: Find the asset behind the finding
levels.primer: Use the named inputs and environment in this level’s practice task. The scenario decision is a separate conceptual check.
levels.experiment: Join scan rows to assets by exact asset ID in inventory.json. Record component, version, owner, exposure and missing values.
levels.variant: Rename a host or move a service and preserve its identity without merging unrelated assets.
levels.control: Include two similar version strings that refer to different products.
levels.recall: Explain why asset identity must precede prioritization.

case.prompt: Two different products expose similar version strings.
case.correct: Establish product identity before applying an advisory.
case.incorrect: Treat matching numbers as the same component.

levels.title: Is the advisory actually applicable?
levels.primer: Use the named inputs and environment in this level’s practice task. The scenario decision is a separate conceptual check.
levels.experiment: Use the explicit LAB-001 condition: notes below 1.1 with sharing enabled. Evaluate A and B, then compare affected.py output.
levels.variant: Change a required feature or version and revise applicability.
levels.control: Include a matching product name with a nonaffected version.
levels.recall: Reconstruct the conditions required before calling the finding applicable.

case.prompt: The advisory's required feature is disabled and unavailable.
case.correct: Verify that condition before deciding applicability.
case.incorrect: A matching product name alone establishes exposure.

levels.title: Prioritize action using context
levels.primer: Use the named inputs and environment in this level’s practice task. The scenario decision is a separate conceptual check.
levels.experiment: Use inventory.json exposure, criticality and fictional exploitation evidence. Apply a written SSVC-style decision path to each item.
levels.variant: Change exposure or exploitation evidence and justify the revised action.
levels.control: Include a high-score isolated lab finding and a lower-score exposed critical asset.
levels.recall: Explain which new evidence would change the highest priority.

case.prompt: A vulnerability has high severity but low exposure on an isolated training asset.
case.correct: Prioritize with exploitation evidence and business context.
case.incorrect: Severity alone dictates the entire remediation queue.

levels.title: Verify the repair rather than the ticket
levels.primer: Use the named inputs and environment in this level’s practice task. The scenario decision is a separate conceptual check.
levels.experiment: In a COPY of inventory.json, model upgrading A to 1.1 or disabling sharing. Run affected.py before and after.
levels.variant: Change the deployment variant and reassess whether the same mitigation applies.
levels.control: Keep a ticket marked resolved from passing when the affected instance still has the old configuration.
levels.recall: Explain patch presence versus effective remediation.

case.prompt: A ticket is closed but the affected instance retains its vulnerable configuration.
case.correct: The repair is not verified on that instance.
case.incorrect: Ticket status is sufficient remediation evidence.

levels.title: Put an expiry date on accepted risk
levels.primer: Use the named inputs and environment in this level’s practice task. The scenario decision is a separate conceptual check.
levels.experiment: Use fictional asset C as temporarily unpatchable because its owner/version is unresolved. Write an exception request with current uncertainty, decision owner and expiry.
levels.variant: Remove a compensating control or change external exposure and reevaluate the exception.
levels.control: Reject an indefinite exception without an accountable owner.
levels.recall: Reconstruct when the exception must return to the remediation queue.

case.prompt: A risk exception has no owner or expiry.
case.correct: Return it for accountable, bounded acceptance.
case.incorrect: Leave it accepted indefinitely.

levels.title: Measure reduction in exposure
levels.primer: Use the named inputs and environment in this level’s practice task. The scenario decision is a separate conceptual check.
levels.experiment: Use a new inventory copy where A is fixed and C now has an owner but still lacks a version.
levels.variant: Add previously unknown assets and revise the metrics without hiding the changed denominator.
levels.control: Distinguish a fall in scan coverage from a real reduction in exposure.
levels.recall: Explain one metric that could look better while security became worse.

case.prompt: Scan coverage drops and the finding count falls.
case.correct: Distinguish lost visibility from reduced exposure.
case.incorrect: Report an improvement without revisiting the denominator.

levels.title: Treat program rules as part of the target
levels.primer: Use the named inputs and environment in this level’s practice task. The scenario decision is a separate conceptual check.
levels.experiment: Use scenario.json scope and rate limit. Write a local-only research question about do_GET ownership or do_PATCH properties.
levels.variant: Add an excluded third-party integration and revise the plan.
levels.control: Identify a technically possible test that the scope disallows.
levels.recall: Explain why a public bug-bounty page does not authorize every asset or technique.

case.prompt: A program excludes a third-party dependency from scope.
case.correct: Do not test that dependency without separate authority.
case.incorrect: A dependency relationship extends the program's permission.

levels.title: Find the invariant the software should preserve
levels.primer: Use the named inputs and environment in this level’s practice task. The scenario decision is a separate conceptual check.
levels.experiment: Trace user input through the selected handler to the note read/update. Mark the exact missing or insufficient check.
levels.variant: Change input encoding or operation order and predict the effect on the invariant.
levels.control: Include a normal edge case that looks unusual but preserves the intended rule.
levels.recall: Reconstruct the vulnerability hypothesis without relying on a scanner label.

case.prompt: A code review suggests a defect with an untested prerequisite.
case.correct: Design a discriminating experiment before claiming impact.
case.incorrect: Report maximum impact as soon as the pattern looks familiar.

levels.title: Make a small test generator teach you something
levels.primer: Use the named inputs and environment in this level’s practice task. The scenario decision is a separate conceptual check.
levels.experiment: Use a bounded generator of at most 20 local cases over note IDs, missing identity and small JSON property names. One request per second; no arbitrary external URL input.
levels.variant: Change the parser or seed corpus and verify the failure still tests the same property.
levels.control: Include malformed input that is correctly rejected and must not count as a vulnerability.
levels.recall: Explain crash, bug, security impact and exploitability as separate claims.

case.prompt: A parser cleanly rejects malformed input.
case.correct: Do not count expected rejection as a security finding.
case.incorrect: Any error response is a vulnerability.

levels.title: Prove only the minimum necessary effect
levels.primer: Use the named inputs and environment in this level’s practice task. The scenario decision is a separate conceptual check.
levels.experiment: Use only the synthetic note data. Show what one unrelated identity can read or alter and the prerequisites needed.
levels.variant: Change the user role or object class and test whether the impact generalizes.
levels.control: Include a failed unauthorized action and avoid claiming access merely from a different response size.
levels.recall: Explain one stronger impact claim the evidence does not support.

case.prompt: A response changes size without evidence of unauthorized data.
case.correct: Investigate further before claiming data access.
case.incorrect: Response size alone proves access to private records.

levels.title: Write a report that survives first triage
levels.primer: Use the named inputs and environment in this level’s practice task. The scenario decision is a separate conceptual check.
levels.experiment: Write a PRIVATE training report with title, affected local fixture/version, scope, minimal requests, actual output, impact limits and tested patch.
levels.variant: Have a peer or fresh environment follow the report with a changed fixture and repair any missing assumption.
levels.control: Keep credentials and live user data out of the evidence packet.
levels.recall: Reconstruct the report's root cause in two precise sentences.

case.prompt: A reproducer contains a real credential.
case.correct: Replace it with synthetic or redacted evidence before sharing.
case.incorrect: Include the credential to make triage easier.

levels.title: Generalize the mechanism carefully
levels.primer: Use the named inputs and environment in this level’s practice task. The scenario decision is a separate conceptual check.
levels.experiment: Switch from the GET ownership case to PATCH mutable properties in a fresh service.py copy. Define the boundary before reusing previous assumptions.
levels.variant: Change one relevant implementation detail and explain why the mechanism applies or fails.
levels.control: Include a superficially similar implementation where the required condition is absent.
levels.recall: Explain which properties transfer and which were accidents of the first target.

case.prompt: A similar component lacks the prerequisite that caused the first bug.
case.correct: Limit the generalization and report the negative control.
case.incorrect: Claim every similar component is vulnerable.

levels.title: Recheck the boundary with a specified change
levels.primer: Use the named task files for the changed case. Predict the effect before opening previous notes.
levels.experiment: In a copy of service.py, repair GET ownership but leave PATCH unrestricted property binding. Test whether the previous root-cause explanation still describes the remaining defect.
levels.variant: Add a second case by reversing the changed condition above, predict its result and compare actual behavior.
levels.control: A text-only owner update should remain valid, and a cross-user GET should now be denied.
levels.recall: Reconstruct why the specified input change did or did not change the outcome. State help used and what remains untested.

experiment_guidance.title: Trace untrusted text into a tool action
experiment_guidance.brief: See where a toy assistant must enforce authorization.

levels.title: Treat generated text as untrusted input
levels.primer: Use the named inputs and environment in this level’s practice task. The scenario decision is a separate conceptual check.
levels.experiment: Use assistant.py and DOCS. Draw user → retrieval → mock model → dispatcher → data and label each trust boundary.
levels.variant: Add an external document source and revise the trust assumptions.
levels.control: Reject the idea that a model's assertion of permission is an authorization decision.
levels.recall: Reconstruct the tool-action boundary without referring to the system prompt.

case.prompt: A model claims the user approved access to a private resource.
case.correct: Enforce authorization in trusted application code.
case.incorrect: Accept the model's statement as the permission check.

levels.title: Keep a document from becoming an instruction
levels.primer: Use the named inputs and environment in this level’s practice task. The scenario decision is a separate conceptual check.
levels.experiment: Use REQUEST_OTHER as instruction-like document content and the public note as a benign input. Record the original mock output and dispatched result.
levels.variant: Change the document wording or source label and verify the same application boundary still holds.
levels.control: Keep a legitimate document answer working and deny a requested unrelated data access.
levels.recall: Explain why prompt wording alone cannot enforce a data-access policy.

case.prompt: A retrieved document contains tool-use instructions.
case.correct: Treat those instructions as untrusted document content.
case.incorrect: Give retrieved instructions authority over the tool policy.

levels.title: Validate what the application will execute
levels.primer: Use the named inputs and environment in this level’s practice task. The scenario decision is a separate conceptual check.
levels.experiment: Define a strict action schema for answer(text) and read(document), rejecting extra privileged fields, unknown actions and wrong value types.
levels.variant: Nest a field or change output encoding and predict whether validation rejects it.
levels.control: Preserve a valid allowed output while rejecting an extra privileged field.
levels.recall: Explain schema validity versus authorization of a valid action.

case.prompt: Generated JSON matches the schema but requests an unauthorized action.
case.correct: Apply authorization after structural validation.
case.incorrect: Schema validity authorizes the requested action.

levels.title: Give an agent a bounded capability
levels.primer: Use the named inputs and environment in this level’s practice task. The scenario decision is a separate conceptual check.
levels.experiment: Make dispatch an explicit allowlist of actions and document identifiers; use DOCS lookups rather than filesystem paths.
levels.variant: Change a resource identifier or attempt a second action outside the allowlist.
levels.control: Permit the intended action and reject traversal-like or unrelated resource references.
levels.recall: Reconstruct where least privilege is enforced independently of the model.

case.prompt: A tool argument refers to a resource outside its allowlist.
case.correct: Reject it independently of the model's explanation.
case.incorrect: Allow it if the model supplies a persuasive rationale.

levels.title: Test retrieval separation between users
levels.primer: Use the named inputs and environment in this level’s practice task. The scenario decision is a separate conceptual check.
levels.experiment: Write tests for alice, bob and public data across DOCS. Enforce ownership before exposing text to mock_model.
levels.variant: Change a document ID, cache key or role and independently retest isolation.
levels.control: Include a shared public document that remains legitimately accessible to both users.
levels.recall: Explain why hiding a private citation after retrieval is too late to guarantee isolation.

case.prompt: Private text is retrieved for the wrong user and hidden only in the final display.
case.correct: Enforce isolation before retrieval and model exposure.
case.incorrect: Hiding the citation repairs the earlier data disclosure.

levels.title: State exactly what the evaluation measured
levels.primer: Use the named inputs and environment in this level’s practice task. The scenario decision is a separate conceptual check.
levels.experiment: Build a labeled suite covering benign answers, own/public document reads, other-user reads, unknown actions and malformed fields.
levels.variant: Add an unseen wording or tool-output shape and rerun the relevant boundary checks.
levels.control: Include benign lookalikes so blocking every input cannot pass the evaluation.
levels.recall: Explain why a passing finite test set does not prove universal prompt-injection resistance.

case.prompt: A deterministic mock pipeline passes every boundary test.
case.correct: Claim the measured application properties and separately evaluate real-model behavior.
case.incorrect: Claim universal resistance to all prompt injection.

levels.primer: Use the named task files for the changed case. Predict the effect before opening previous notes.
levels.experiment: Change mock_model to emit an extra privileged field inside a nested output object. Add a new instruction-like phrase that requests the same forbidden document and rerun boundary checks.
levels.variant: Add a second case by reversing the changed condition above, predict its result and compare actual behavior.
levels.control: Keep the valid public answer and same-user retrieval working; refusing every generated output cannot pass.
levels.recall: Reconstruct why the specified input change did or did not change the outcome. State help used and what remains untested.
